# Generalized synthetic control {#sec-gsynth}

```{r .common, include = FALSE}
source("_common.R")
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
The standalone **gsynth** package is a wrapper of **fect**. Use its [old syntax](https://yiqingxu.org/packages/gsynth/) if needed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
### TL;DR

- GSC estimates factors from never-treated controls, then uses each treated unit's pretreatment outcomes to estimate its loadings. In **fect**, set `method = "gsynth"`.
- Use GSC for block or staggered adoption without treatment reversal, including panels with few treated units.
- Follow the five checks in [Section @sec-gsynth-checks]: count the data; check overlap; choose the rank forward from treated units; use out-of-sample inference; report the choices.
- Rolling CV remains the default of `CV = TRUE`, but for GSC it scores control cells and can miss a factor on which treated and control units differ. Choose the rank with the forward rule (Step 3).
- Bounded factor loadings (`loading.bound = "simplex"`) are optional and do not replace the overlap checks.
- Basic estimation comes first. Cross-validation options, plots, staggered adoption, unbalanced panels, bounded loadings, and inference follow the five checks.
:::

GSC is the generalized synthetic control method proposed in @Xu2017 \[<a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/generalized-synthetic-control-method-causal-inference-with-interactive-fixed-effects-models/B63A8BD7C239DD4141C67DA10CD0E4F3" target="_blank">Paper</a>\]. Download the R script for this chapter [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuyiqing/fect/dev/vignettes/rscript/06-gsynth.R).

GSC differs from the other estimators in **fect** in its treatment setting, factor estimation, and inference:

- GSC handles block and staggered DID without treatment reversal. FEct, IFEct, and MC also allow reversals under assumptions about carryover effects.
- GSC can be used with few treated units. Its parametric bootstrap uses prediction errors from controls left out of the factor fit.
- GSC estimates time components from never-treated controls. IFE-EM uses all untreated cells, including treated units' pretreatment observations.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
### Equivalent specifications

`fect(..., method = "gsynth")` is equivalent to `fect(..., method = "ife", time.component.from = "nevertreated")`.

Both fit an interactive fixed effects (IFE) model with factors estimated from never-treated controls. Each treated unit's loadings are then estimated from its own pretreatment outcomes.
:::

Use `method = "gsynth"` when treatment does not reverse and never-treated controls are available. This includes settings with $N_{tr} = 1$. Set `vartype = "parametric"` explicitly to use the parametric bootstrap.

The default IFE-EM regime, `time.component.from = "notyettreated"`, uses EM to estimate time components from all untreated cells. It accommodates treatment reversal ([Chapter @sec-fect]).

The examples use `sim_gsynth` for block adoption and `turnout` for staggered adoption.

```{r setup-seed, echo = FALSE}
set.seed(1234)
```

```{r load-packages, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
data(sim_gsynth)
data(turnout)
ls()
```

## Basic usage

The simulated example shows the data structure, estimation arguments, and returned estimates.

### Simulated data

`sim_gsynth` is the simulated dataset described in @Xu2017. It has 5 treated units, 45 control units, and 30 time periods. Treatment starts in Period 21 for every treated unit, giving a block DID design.

```{r head-sim_gsynth}
head(sim_gsynth)
```

Use **panelView** to inspect treatment timing and missing observations. The plot shows that (1) there are 5 treated units and 45 controls; (2) treatment starts in period 21; and (3) there are no missing values.

```{r sim-panelview-status, cache = FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.width=7, warning=FALSE}
library(panelView)
panelview(Y ~ D, data = sim_gsynth,  index = c("id","time"), pre.post = TRUE) 
```

The outcome plot colors each path by treatment status.

```{r sim-panelview-outcome, cache = FALSE,fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
panelview(Y ~ D, data = sim_gsynth,  index = c("id","time"), type = "outcome") 
```

### Estimation

The outcome is $Y$, the treatment indicator is $D$, and the covariates are $X_1$ and $X_2$. The unit and time identifiers are $id$ and $time$.

Set `method = "gsynth"` to fit GSC. This first call illustrates the default CV interface. For the recommended rank choice, use the forward rule in [Section @sec-gsynth-checks].

```{r sim2, cache = TRUE}
system.time(
out <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id","time"), 
            method = "gsynth", force = "two-way", CV = TRUE, r = c(0, 5), 
            se = TRUE, nboots = 1000, vartype = 'parametric', 
            parallel = TRUE, cores = 16))
```

The first variable on the right-hand side is the binary treatment indicator. The remaining variables are covariates. `index` identifies the unit and time columns.

`force` selects the additive fixed effects: `"none"`, `"unit"`, `"time"`, or `"two-way"`. The default, `"two-way"`, includes unit and time effects.

With `CV = TRUE`, `r=c(0,5)` sets the candidate rank range. With `CV = FALSE`, the first element of `r` fixes the rank. A scalar also works, such as $r = 0$.

Set `se = TRUE` to estimate uncertainty. With few treated units, use `vartype = "parametric"` subject to the cautions in the five checks. Conformal intervals (`vartype = "conformal"`) offer a finite-sample guarantee under their exchangeability and tuning conditions; see [Chapter @sec-conformal]. The default number of parametric bootstrap runs is 200. Change it with `nboots`.

The printed output includes `sigma2`, the estimated error variance; `IC`, an information criterion; and `MSPE`, the mean squared prediction error. By default (`cv.rule = "min"`), CV selects the rank with the smallest MSPE. `cv.rule = "1se"` selects the smallest rank within one standard error of it.

The following fields report three commonly requested results:

- `est.att`: average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) by event time.
- `est.avg`: ATT averaged over treated post-treatment observations.
- `beta`: coefficients of the time-varying covariates.

```{r print-results, eval = FALSE}
print(out)
out$est.att
out$est.avg
out$beta
```

`att.boot` stores the bootstrap ATT estimates, with one row per event time and one column per run. With `keep.sims = TRUE`, `eff.boot` also stores cell-level draws (time periods \* units \* bootstrap runs).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Use `cores` to set the number of parallel workers for CV and uncertainty estimation. If `cores` is omitted or `NULL`, **fect** selects the smaller of `8` and the number of usable system cores minus `2`.
:::

## Five checks for a GSC analysis {#sec-gsynth-checks}

@iwasakixu2026overlap reanalyze published applications of GSC and IFE-EM and recommend five steps, in order: count the data, check overlap before choosing the rank, choose the rank forward from the treated units, use out-of-sample inference, and report what was done. Version 2.5.0 of **fect** runs each step. This section walks through them on `sim_gsynth`.

### Step 1: count the data

GSC predicts a treated unit's untreated outcome from the factors of the never-treated units and the unit's own pretreatment periods, so count both. `sim_gsynth` has 45 never-treated units and 5 treated units, each with 20 pretreatment periods. The rank rule of Step 3 needs about 15 pretreatment periods when the candidate ranks go up to 5. With fewer, report the ranks that both rules of Step 3 pick (forward and leave one out), and treat a finding that holds at some ranks and not at others as fragile. `fect_rank()` reports whether the window is long enough (see Step 3).

### Step 2: check overlap before choosing the rank

A factor model can only predict a treated unit well if the controls can represent it. `overlap_check()` asks this of the raw data, before any model is fitted. For each treated unit, it takes the unit's pretreatment periods, subtracts from the treated unit's path and from each never-treated unit's path its mean over those periods, rebuilds the treated unit's path as a weighted average of the never-treated units' paths (weights that are non-negative and sum to one), and records the root mean squared error. The yardstick is the same error for each never-treated unit rebuilt from the others. A treated unit is flagged when its error is larger than the donors' 90th percentile.

```{r gsc-check-overlap}
oc <- overlap_check(Y ~ D, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"), level = 0.90)
oc
```

One of the five treated units, unit 105, is rebuilt worse than 93% of the donors and is flagged. The table `oc$units` gives each unit's error, its percentile (`pct`) and its weight in the average effect. The check needs no rank and no factor model, so the choice of the rank cannot change it. It is a screen rather than a test. A treated unit is rebuilt from all the donors, while each donor is rebuilt from the others, so the treated unit's error tends to be smaller, and a unit slightly outside what the donors can reproduce may pass. Like every pretreatment check, it cannot detect a factor that does not vary before treatment starts. `plot(oc)` draws each treated unit's gap, its demeaned pretreatment outcome minus its rebuild, in each period before adoption.

```{r gsc-check-overlap-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5}
plot(oc)
```

The grey lines are the donors' gaps, each donor rebuilt from the others, and the shaded region holds 90% of them in each period. A unit the donors can follow has a gap that stays mostly inside the region and crosses zero at random. A gap that leaves the region often, or that trends or stays on one side of zero near adoption, belongs to a unit the donors cannot follow. Unit 105's gap leaves the region in 6 of its 20 periods, against 1 to 3 for the other units, and its region is pink because it is flagged. `plot(oc, type = "percentile")` draws one row per unit, which suits panels with many treated units.

### Step 3: choose the rank forward from the treated units

`fect_rank()` fits GSC at every candidate rank and scores each rank by how well it predicts the treated units' own pretreatment outcomes. The forward rule refits each treated unit's loadings on its first pretreatment periods and predicts the next one, moving the cutoff forward one period at a time, so every prediction uses only earlier periods, as the post-treatment prediction does. The leave-one-out rule of @Xu2017 also trains on later periods, which under serially correlated errors carry information about the held-out one, so it leans toward more factors. The chosen rank is the smallest minimizer of the forward score. The table also gives the estimate at every rank and the share of the treated units' predicted post-treatment outcomes that lie outside the range of all observed outcomes in the panel (`extrapolation`).

```{r gsc-check-rank, cache = TRUE}
rk <- fect_rank(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"),
                force = "two-way", r = 0:5)
rk
```

The forward rule picks 2 factors, the number in the simulation, and so does the leave-one-out rule. Report the estimate at every candidate rank and mark the one the rule chose. Here it moves between 5.54 and 5.81 from r = 1 on, a range of about one standard error (0.26 in the output below). To fit at the forward rule's rank in one call, set `cv.method = "forward"`:

```{r gsc-check-forward, cache = TRUE}
out.fwd <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"),
                method = "gsynth", force = "two-way", CV = TRUE, r = c(0, 5),
                cv.method = "forward", se = TRUE, vartype = "parametric",
                nboots = 500, seed = 1234, parallel = TRUE, cores = 16)
out.fwd$r.cv
out.fwd$est.avg
```

At the chosen rank, `loading_check()` checks overlap in the factor model itself. It asks whether each treated unit's estimated loading lies inside the region the controls' loadings enclose (their convex hull). For a unit outside the hull, it measures the distance to the hull relative to the sampling variance of the unit's own loading estimate, and flags the unit when that distance exceeds the 95th percentile of a chi-square distribution with r degrees of freedom. With `trim = TRUE` it drops the flagged units, chooses the rank again on the units kept and refits. Report the trimmed estimate beside the full one. It is the effect for the treated units the controls can represent, a different estimand.

```{r gsc-check-loading, cache = TRUE}
lc <- loading_check(out.fwd, trim = TRUE)
lc
```

Three of the five treated units, unit 105 among them, lie outside the hull, but each by less than the noise in its loadings allows (`lc$table`). None is flagged, so there is nothing to trim. Step 2 flags unit 105 and this check does not, because the two checks ask different questions, and each can flag a unit the other passes. `plot(lc)` draws the loadings.

```{r gsc-check-loading-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(lc)
```

### Step 4: use out-of-sample inference

With few treated units, use the parametric bootstrap (`vartype = "parametric"`, Algorithm 2 of @Xu2017, as in `out.fwd` above). It simulates each treated unit's prediction error with the prediction errors of controls left out of the factor fit. Use it with caution when the controls are few relative to the treated units or to the rank. The interval at the chosen rank does not account for the choice of the rank. Conformal intervals are a second option, with a finite-sample guarantee under their own conditions ([Section @sec-gsynth-conformal]).

For IFE-EM (`method = "ife"`, factors from all untreated cells), Algorithm 2 does not apply, because the factors depend on the treated units' own pretreatment errors, and `vartype = "parametric"` stops with an error. With few treated units, use GSC with Algorithm 2, or conformal intervals, which also work with IFE-EM ([Section @sec-gsynth-conformal]). The unit bootstrap and the jackknife rely on variation across treated units and do not solve the problem when there are few.

### Step 5: report

Report the rank and how it was chosen (here, the forward rule over ranks 0 to 5), whether a printed estimate is an average or a single period, the version of **fect**, the stopping rule (`tol`, `max.iteration`) and the seed, and post the data and code.

## Cross-validation

`cv.method = "rolling"` is the default for DID/TWFE CV, GSC CV, and `fect_mspe()`. `"block"` is also available. For GSC rank selection, the five checks recommend `"forward"` instead.

| | `fect_cv` (DID/TWFE) | CV in GSC | `fect_mspe` (post-hoc) |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `"rolling"` | **Default** | **Default** | **Default** |
| `"block"` | Available | Available | Available |
| `"loo"` | --- | Available | --- |
| `"forward"` | --- | Available (v2.5.0) | --- |

The methods differ in what they predict and which periods they use:

- `"rolling"` holds out blocks and drops later eligible periods from each sampled unit's training data.
- `"block"` holds out blocks while retaining eligible periods on both sides.
- `"loo"` predicts each treated unit's pretreatment outcomes from its other pretreatment periods.
- `"forward"` predicts each treated unit's pretreatment outcomes from earlier periods only. It does not mask cells in the control factor fit.

`"loo"` and `"forward"` require `time.component.from = "nevertreated"`. Their factor estimates must exclude the held-out treated observations. For GSC, rolling and block CV score control cells. A factor that matters more for treated units can receive little weight in those scores. Changing the window does not resolve that problem [@iwasakixu2026overlap]. Use `fect_rank()` and the forward rule in [Section @sec-gsynth-checks].

The legacy values `"all_units"` (now `"block"`) and `"treated_units"` (block masking restricted to treated pretreatment cells) remain accepted and print a note. Use `"block"` in place of `"all_units"`. See the [cheatsheet](aa-cheatsheet.html#sec-cheatsheet-cv).

The following call shows the rolling-window option. Its selected rank is an alternative to compare with the treated-unit rules. See [Chapter @sec-ife-mc] for the rolling design and the side-by-side figure.

```{r rcv_dispatcher_gsc, eval = FALSE}
fit <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"),
            method = "gsynth", force = "two-way",
            CV = TRUE, r = c(0, 5),
            cv.method = "rolling",
            cv.buffer = 1, cv.nobs = 3, k = 20, cv.prop = 0.1,
            cv.rule = "1se",
            se = TRUE, vartype = "parametric")
fit$r.cv     # selected r --- use this for downstream inference
```

Rolling and block CV score the model's full prediction for both `method = "ife"` and `method = "gsynth"`. That prediction includes the intercept, unit and time effects, covariates, and factors. The estimators differ in which observations supply their time components. See the [Cross-Validation section of the cheatsheet](aa-cheatsheet.html#sec-cheatsheet-cv) for the parameter reference.

## Plot reference

The plots below use `out`, the initial fit with default rolling CV. They illustrate plot options. The five-check analysis uses `out.fwd`.

### Gap plots

`plot(out)` reports ATT by event time. The true effects in `sim_gsynth` range from 1 to 10, with added white noise, during periods 21 to 30.

`plot()` returns a **ggplot2** object. `print()` displays it, and `ggsave()` saves it.

```{r sim_gap1, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
a <- plot(out) # by default, type = "gap"
print(a)
```

`connected = TRUE` draws the confidence interval as a shaded area.

```{r sim-gap-connected, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out, connected = TRUE)
```

`show.points = FALSE` removes the points.

```{r sim-gap-line, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out, connected = TRUE, show.points = FALSE)
```

Use `main` for the title, `xlab` and `ylab` for axis labels, and `xlim` and `ylim` for axis limits. Standard **ggplot2** styling also applies.

```{r sim_gap2, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "gap", ylim = c(-6,12), xlab = "Period", 
     main = "Estimated ATT (Gsynth)")
```

### Plot types

The eight plot types used here are:

- `"gap"`: ATT by event time (the default).
- `"counterfactual"`: average observed treated outcomes and estimated untreated outcomes.
- `"factors"`: estimated factors.
- `"loadings"`: estimated factor loadings.
- `"status"`: treatment and observation status. `axis.lab` selects labels. With 200 or more units, unit labels are dropped.
- `"box"`: distributions of estimated unit-level gaps.
- `"calendar"`: ATT by calendar time.
- `"equiv"`: average pretreatment residuals with equivalence confidence intervals.

For `method = "gsynth"` with `vartype = "parametric"`, the counterfactual plot's 95% intervals have the same widths as the ATT intervals, reflected around the observed outcomes.

```{r sim-counterfactual, cache = FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "counterfactual")
```

`raw = "all"` adds each treated and control unit's observed outcome path.

```{r sim-counterfactual-all, cache = FALSE,fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "counterfactual", raw = "all")
```

`raw = "band"` adds the 5th to 95th percentiles of observed treated and control outcomes in each period. The bands describe the raw outcomes. They are not confidence intervals.

```{r sim-counterfactual-band, cache = FALSE,fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "counterfactual", raw = "band")
```

`"status"` shows treatment status. Use `xticklabels` and `yticklabels` to select labels, such as `xticklabels=c("1","5","10", "15","20", "25", "30")`. A nonexistent value, such as `yticklabels="0"`, removes numeric labels on that axis. **panelView** provides a standalone version.

```{r sim_status, cache = FALSE,fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "status", yticklabels="0", 
     xticklabels=c("5", "10", "15","20", "25", "30") )
```

`"loadings"` and `"factors"` display the fitted factor model.

```{r sim_L, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE, results='hide', fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "loadings")
```

```{r sim_F, message = FALSE, results='hide', fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "factors", xlab = "Time")
```

`"box"` shows the dispersion of estimated unit-level gaps. These gaps include prediction error and do not by themselves identify individual treatment effects. With few treated units, the display becomes a scatter plot. The graph labels the number of treated units; `xangle` and `yangle` tilt axis labels.

```{r sim_box, cache = FALSE,fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
plot(out, type = "box", xlab = "time",
     xticklabels=c("-19", "-15", "-10", "-5","0","5","10") )
```

`xlim` restricts the display, here to fifteen periods before treatment and ten after.

```{r sim_box2, eval = FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
plot(out, type = "box", xlim = c(-15, 10), 
     xticklabels=c( "-15", "-10", "-5","0","5","10"))
```

`"calendar"` shows ATT by calendar time. The blue lowess curve has a shaded 95% confidence band, and the red dashed line marks the overall average ATT.

```{r calendar, cache = FALSE,fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out,type = "calendar")
```

## Staggered DID

The `turnout` example examines Election-Day Registration (EDR) reforms in the United States. Treatment starts in different periods across states. See @Xu2017 Section 5 for the dataset.

### Data structure

The **panelView** plot shows that (1) the panel is balanced with 9 treated units and (2) treatment starts in different periods.

```{r turnout-panelview-status, cache = FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=10, fig.width=7}
panelview(turnout ~ policy_edr, data = turnout, 
          index = c("abb","year"), pre.post = TRUE, 
          by.timing = TRUE) 
```

The outcome plot colors paths by treatment status.

```{r turnout-panelview-outcome, cache = FALSE, warning =FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
panelview(turnout ~ policy_edr, data = turnout,
          index = c("abb","year"), type = "outcome", 
          main = "EDR Reform and Turnout")
```

### Estimation without factors

Without factors, the ATT estimates are close to the difference-in-differences estimates.

```{r turnout_did, cache = TRUE}
out0 <- fect(turnout ~ policy_edr + policy_mail_in + policy_motor, 
               data = turnout, index = c("abb","year"), 
               se = TRUE, method = "gsynth",
               r = 0, CV = FALSE, force = "two-way", 
               nboots = 1000, seed = 02139)
```

```{r turnout_did_gap, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out0, type = "gap", xlim = c(-15, 5), ylim=c(-15, 10))
```

### Estimation with factors

This call retains the default CV specification for comparison. For a GSC analysis, use `fect_rank()` to compare ranks and choose forward from the treated units, as in [Section @sec-gsynth-checks].

Set `keep.sims = TRUE` to retain the draws needed for counterfactual intervals for subsets of treated units.

```{r turnout_est, cache = TRUE}
out_turnout <- fect(turnout ~ policy_edr + policy_mail_in + policy_motor, 
              data = turnout,  index = c("abb","year"), 
              se = TRUE, method = "gsynth", vartype = "parametric",
              r = c(0, 5), CV = TRUE, force = "two-way", 
              nboots = 1000, seed = 02139, keep.sims = TRUE)
```

### Implied weights

`wgt.implied` stores an $N_{co}\times N_{tr}$ matrix, with one row per control unit and one column per treated unit. Unit IDs label the rows and columns. Column $i$ holds weights that rebuild the factor part of treated unit $i$'s counterfactual:

$$
\Lambda_{co}^\top w_i = \lambda_i,\qquad
w_i = \Lambda_{co}(\Lambda_{co}^\top\Lambda_{co})^{-1}\lambda_i.
$$

These weights can be positive or negative [@Xu2017]. With time fixed effects, each column sums to zero. They represent the factor component, rather than synthetic-control weights for the full outcome. The following output shows Wisconsin's weights.

```{r turnout-implied-weights}
dim(out_turnout$wgt.implied)
sort(out_turnout$wgt.implied[, "WI"])
```

### Plot reference

The gap plot reports ATT by event time.

```{r turnout_gap, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out_turnout, xlim = c(-10, 5), ylim=c(-10, 10))
```

The status plot shows staggered adoption. `xlab`, `ylab`, and `main` set labels, and `xangle` and `yangle` set their tilt in degrees.

```{r turnout-status-plot, fig.height=12, fig.width=7}
plot(out_turnout, type = "status",xlab = "Year", ylab = "State", main = "Treatment Status", 
     xticklabels=c(1920, 1928, 1936, 1944, 1952, 1960, 
                   1968, 1976, 1984, 1992, 2000, 2008), xangle=10)
```

The counterfactual plot compares observed and estimated untreated outcomes.

```{r turnout_counterfactual, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out_turnout, type = "counterfactual")
```

`id` selects a state or a vector of states. Subset counterfactual intervals require `keep.sims = TRUE` and `vartype = "parametric"` in this example.

```{r turnout_gap2, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out_turnout, type = "counterfactual", id = "WI", main = "Wisconsin")
```

With few treated units, the box plot becomes a scatter plot.

```{r turnout_box, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out_turnout, type = "box", 
     xticklabels=c("-20", "-15", "-10", "-5","0","5","10"))
```

The calendar plot reports ATT by calendar time.

```{r turnout_calendar, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out_turnout, type = "calendar", ylim = c(-15,15))
```

The factor and loading plots describe the fitted factor model.

```{r turnout_F, message = FALSE, results = 'hide', fig.height=5, fig.width=7, warning=FALSE}
plot(out_turnout, type = "factors", xlab = "Year")
```

```{r turnout_L, message = FALSE, results = 'hide', fig.height=7, fig.width=7, warning=FALSE}
plot(out_turnout, type = "loadings")
```

### Cumulative effects

For staggered adoption without reversals, cumulative ATT sums the per-period ATTs from event time 1 to $k$. Use it when the sum answers the substantive question, such as accumulated voter mobilization. `out_turnout` retains the cell-level replicates needed by `estimand()` because it uses `keep.sims = TRUE` and `vartype = "parametric"`.

```{r turnout-cumulative, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
cumu.turnout <- estimand(out_turnout, "att.cumu", "event.time")
esplot(cumu.turnout, Period = "event.time",
       Estimate = "estimate", CI.lower = "ci.lo", CI.upper = "ci.hi",
       Count = "n_cells",
       main = "Cumulative Effect of EDR Reform on Turnout",
       ylab = "Cumulative ATT")
```

See [Chapter @sec-estimands] (Alternative Estimands) for `estimand()`, including parametric variance, log-scale ATT, and APTT.

## Unbalanced panels

GSC in **fect** accommodates unbalanced panels. This example removes 50 observations at random and the first 15 observations of Wyoming, then refits the model.

```{r create-unbalanced-data}
set.seed(123456)
turnout.ub <- turnout[-c(which(turnout$abb=="WY")[1:15], 
                         sample(1:nrow(turnout),50,replace=FALSE)),]
```

White cells in the **panelView** plot mark missing observations.

```{r turnout_ub_panelview_miss, cache = FALSE,fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
panelview(turnout ~ policy_edr + policy_mail_in + policy_motor, 
          data = turnout.ub,  index = c("abb","year"), 
          pre.post = TRUE) 
```

### Estimation

The first fit uses the default unit bootstrap. It is retained to compare with the explicit parametric-bootstrap fit below. Both calls use default CV. In an analysis, apply the five checks before choosing a rank.

```{r turnout_ub_est, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE}
out_ub <- fect(turnout ~ policy_edr + policy_mail_in + policy_motor,
              data = turnout.ub,  index = c("abb","year"),
              se = TRUE, method = "gsynth",
              r = c(0, 5), CV = TRUE, force = "two-way",
              parallel = TRUE, cores = 16, min.T0 = 8,
              nboots = 1000, seed = 02139)
```

### Parametric bootstrap on an unbalanced panel

With few treated units, the five checks recommend the GSC parametric bootstrap, subject to the cautions in Step 4. Set `vartype = "parametric"` explicitly. It is also available when outcomes are missing.

On a balanced panel, the default parametric-bootstrap path resamples whole-$T$ error vectors. With missing outcomes (`para.error = "ar"`, the default there), **fect** uses Gaussian draws based on pairwise-available residual second moments. It retains off-diagonal terms to represent within-unit serial dependence. These are estimated second moments; the draws need not reproduce the full error distribution.

The parametric bootstrap targets uncertainty conditional on the factors, loadings, covariates, and treatment indicators, $(\Lambda, F, X, D)$. The unit bootstrap resamples unit identities and reflects variation in sample composition. Their standard errors need not coincide. See [Chapter @sec-inference] for its mechanics.

```{r turnout_ub_param, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE}
out_ub_param <- fect(turnout ~ policy_edr + policy_mail_in + policy_motor,
                     data = turnout.ub, index = c("abb","year"),
                     se = TRUE, method = "gsynth", vartype = "parametric",
                     r = c(0, 5), CV = TRUE, force = "two-way",
                     parallel = TRUE, cores = 16, min.T0 = 8,
                     nboots = 1000, seed = 02139)
```

Compare the average widths of the period-specific ATT intervals. Similar widths would not establish that either procedure has correct coverage.

```{r turnout_ub_ci_compare}
ci_width <- function(out) mean(out$est.att[, "CI.upper"] -
                                out$est.att[, "CI.lower"], na.rm = TRUE)
data.frame(
  vartype  = c("bootstrap", "parametric"),
  CI_width = c(ci_width(out_ub), ci_width(out_ub_param))
)
```

### Plot reference

The fitted status plot marks Wyoming in gray because it has too few pretreatment observations and is excluded.

`out_ub$obs.missing` records observation status: 1 for treated observations, 2 for untreated observations, 3 for missing observations, and 4 for excluded units. Fits with placebo or carryover tests also use 5 for masked test observations and 6 for observations removed by `carryover.rm`.

```{r, turnout_ub_panelview_miss2, fig.height=12, fig.width=7}
plot(out_ub, type = "status",
     xticklabels=c(1920, 1928, 1936, 1944, 1952, 1960, 
                   1968, 1976, 1984, 1992, 2000, 2008),
     xangle=10)
```

Use `id` to select units and the axis options to adjust the display.

```{r turnout_ub_obs_2, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
plot(out_ub, type = "status", xlab = "Year", ylab = "State",
     main = "Treatment Status", id = out_ub$id[out_ub$tr],
     xlim = c(1920,2012), 
     xticklabels=c(1920, 1928, 1936, 1944, 1952, 1960,
                   1968, 1976, 1984, 1992, 2000, 2008))

```

The unit-bootstrap gap plot uses a y-axis range of $(-10,15)$.

```{r turnout_ub_gap, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out_ub, type = "gap", xlim = c(-10, 5), ylim = c(-10, 15))
```

The next plot uses the parametric bootstrap on the same unbalanced panel.

```{r turnout_ub_gap_param, fig.height=5, fig.width=7}
plot(out_ub_param, type = "gap", xlim = c(-10, 5), ylim = c(-10, 15))
```

## Bounded factor loadings

`loading.bound = "simplex"` constrains each treated loading to a non-negative weighted average of control loadings. The default, `"none"`, estimates treated loadings by unconstrained least squares.

The bound changes the estimator. It does not establish that the controls can represent a treated unit. Follow the five checks first. `overlap_check()` screens the raw pretreatment paths, and `loading_check()` assesses estimated loadings at the chosen rank. If units are flagged, report the trimmed estimate beside the full estimate.

### The simplex projection

For each treated unit $i$, the bounded estimator solves

$$
\min_{w_i \in \Delta^{N_{co}}} \;\; \frac{1}{\gamma} \, \mathrm{KL}(w_i \,\|\, \tilde{w}) \; + \; \big\| u_i^{\mathrm{pre}} - F^{\mathrm{pre}} \Lambda_{co}^\top w_i \big\|_2^2
$$

where:

- $w_i$ is the $N_{co}$-vector of weights, with $w_{ij} \geq 0$ and $\sum_j w_{ij} = 1$;
- $\tilde{w} = (1/N_{co}, \ldots, 1/N_{co})$ is the uniform reference, and $\mathrm{KL}(w \,\|\, \tilde{w}) = \sum_j w_j \log(N_{co}\, w_j)$ penalizes departures from it;
- $\gamma > 0$ controls regularization: as $\gamma \to \infty$, the penalty vanishes; as $\gamma \to 0$, the weights approach uniform;
- $u_i^{\mathrm{pre}}$ is the pretreatment outcome after removing the grand mean, covariate contribution, and any time effects. It still contains the unit's own level;
- $F^{\mathrm{pre}}$ is the $T_0 \times r$ matrix of estimated pretreatment factors;
- $\Lambda_{co}$ is the $N_{co} \times r$ matrix of estimated control loadings.

The fitted loading is $\hat\lambda_i = \Lambda_{co}^\top w_i$. Its factor component,

$$
F\,\hat\lambda_i = F\Lambda_{co}^\top w_i,
$$

lies pointwise in the convex hull of the control factor components. The full counterfactual also includes the additive effects and covariate contribution. The bound therefore does not put the full counterfactual inside the range of observed control outcomes.

The objective combines pretreatment squared error with a penalty toward uniform weights. Without a unit effect, the solver uses a softmax parameterization and `optim(method = "L-BFGS-B")`, with an analytic gradient. A mirror-descent fallback handles ill-conditioned inputs. With a unit effect, the centered problem uses Newton's method on the dual, with L-BFGS-B as the fallback.

#### The unit intercept

With `force = "unit"` or `"two-way"`, each treated unit has a free intercept $\alpha_i$. Since version 2.4.8, the estimator fits it jointly with the weights:

$$
\min_{\alpha_i \in \mathbb{R},\; w_i \in \Delta^{N_{co}}} \;\; \frac{1}{\gamma} \, \mathrm{KL}(w_i \,\|\, \tilde{w}) \; + \; \big\| u_i^{\mathrm{pre}} - \alpha_i \mathbf{1} - F^{\mathrm{pre}} \Lambda_{co}^\top w_i \big\|_2^2 .
$$

For given weights, the best intercept is the pretreatment mean of $u_i^{\mathrm{pre}} - F^{\mathrm{pre}}\Lambda_{co}^\top w_i$. The solver therefore centers the outcome and factors over each treated unit's pretreatment periods, fits the weights, then recovers the intercept. The intercept is not bounded. CV for $\gamma$ centers within each training fold and predicts with that fold's intercept.

Adding a constant to a treated unit's outcome changes only its intercept. Its weights, loadings, and ATT stay the same. With `force = "none"` or `"time"`, there is no unit intercept, and the solver uses the uncentered objective.

### Bounded and unbounded fits

Set `loading.bound = "simplex"` to activate the bound. By default, 5-fold CV over a log-grid selects $\gamma$. Set `gamma.loading` to fix it, or use `gamma.loading.grid` to supply the grid. This tuning selects the penalty strength, separately from the rank.

The bound is available for `method = "gsynth"`, equivalently `method = "ife", time.component.from = "nevertreated"`. The following fits hold the rank and other settings fixed.

```{r bounded-vs-unbounded-fit, eval = TRUE, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE, results = "hide"}
# Unbounded gsynth (default v2.2.x behavior --- standard Xu 2017 estimator)
out.unbounded <- fect(Y ~ D, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"),
                      method = "gsynth", r = 2,
                      se = TRUE, vartype = "parametric", nboots = 100,
                      CV = FALSE, parallel = FALSE, seed = 1234)

# Bounded gsynth (new in v2.3.0 --- simplex projection)
out.bounded   <- fect(Y ~ D, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"),
                      method = "gsynth", r = 2,
                      loading.bound = "simplex",
                      se = TRUE, vartype = "parametric", nboots = 100,
                      CV = FALSE, parallel = FALSE, seed = 1234)
```

The output compares ATT estimates and reports the selected penalty and pretreatment projection residuals.

```{r bounded-vs-unbounded-att}
cat("Unbounded ATT =", round(out.unbounded$att.avg, 3), "\n")
cat("Bounded   ATT =", round(out.bounded$att.avg,   3), "\n")
cat("\ngamma.loading (CV-selected) =", round(out.bounded$gamma.loading, 4), "\n")
cat("\nPer-treated projection residuals (loading.proj.resid):\n")
print(round(out.bounded$loading.proj.resid, 3))
```

Large `loading.proj.resid` values relative to the control-fit RMSE indicate poor pretreatment fit under the bound. They are not the noise-adjusted distances reported by `loading_check()`. When the constraint binds, percentile-bootstrap intervals may under-cover.

#### Gap plots

The gap plots compare the estimated effects under the two specifications.

```{r bounded-vs-unbounded-gap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4, message = FALSE}
library(gridExtra)
gap.un  <- plot(out.unbounded, type = "gap", main = "Unbounded gsynth")
gap.bd  <- plot(out.bounded,   type = "gap", main = "Bounded gsynth (simplex)")
grid.arrange(gap.un, gap.bd, ncol = 2)
```

#### Loading overlap plots

`loading.overlap` plots factor 1 against factor 2. The shaded hull contains the control loadings, and red triangles mark treated loadings. The unbounded plot shows the estimated treated loadings. The bounded plot shows loadings constrained to lie inside or on the hull.

Use `loading_check()` on the unbounded fit to assess whether distances outside the hull exceed each treated loading's estimated noise, as in Step 3. The plot shows where the loadings lie. The check also accounts for their estimation noise. A bounded plot cannot establish overlap because the constraint puts the loadings inside the hull.

```{r bounded-vs-unbounded-overlap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4}
ov.un <- plot(out.unbounded, type = "loading.overlap",
              main = "Unbounded loadings")
ov.bd <- plot(out.bounded,   type = "loading.overlap",
              main = "Bounded loadings (projected)")
grid.arrange(ov.un, ov.bd, ncol = 2)
```

For a one-factor model ($r = 1$), the plot uses a mirror histogram. Treated counts appear above the axis and control counts below. A band marks the control range, the 1D counterpart of the hull.

#### Implicit donor weights

The weights in `wgt.implied` represent each treated unit's factor component as a linear combination of control factor components. The matrix has dimensions $N_{co} \times N_{tr}$, with one column per treated unit.

Without the bound, the weights use the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse,

$$
w_i = \Lambda_{co}(\Lambda_{co}^\top\Lambda_{co})^{-1}\lambda_i.
$$

They can be negative and, with time fixed effects, sum to zero. With the simplex bound, each column is non-negative and sums to one. The scatter pairs the unbounded and bounded weights for each treated-control pair.

```{r bounded-vs-unbounded-weights, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
W.un <- as.matrix(out.unbounded$wgt.implied)
W.bd <- as.matrix(out.bounded$wgt.implied)
df.w <- data.frame(
  unbounded = as.numeric(W.un),
  bounded   = as.numeric(W.bd)
)

ggplot(df.w, aes(x = unbounded, y = bounded)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              color = "grey60", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.4, color = "#3F6A99") +
  labs(x = "Unbounded weight (Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse)",
       y = "Bounded weight (simplex-projected)",
       title = "Implicit donor weights: bounded vs unbounded",
       subtitle = "One point per (treated, control) pair; dashed line is y = x") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The plot shows these patterns:

- **Many bounded weights are near $y = 0$.** Of the treated-control pairs, 48% have bounded weights below 0.001. Four of the five treated units put weights above 0.01 on 16 or fewer of the 45 controls. The five counts are 41, 16, 11, 8 and 2. The simplex permits concentration on a few donors; the entropy penalty pushes toward uniform weights $(1/N_{co})$. As $\gamma \to 0$, weights approach uniform.
- **Donors with negative unbounded weights often receive small bounded weights.** Among the 118 negative unbounded weights, the largest bounded counterpart is 0.020, and 83% are below 0.01. The bound excludes negative weights, but it refits all weights jointly rather than truncating them.
- **The largest bounded weights go to donors with positive unbounded weights.** The 11 points above $y = 0.1$ are among the four largest unbounded weights for their treated unit. For the fourth and fifth treated units, the three largest bounded weights sum to 0.81 and 1.00. For the first unit, the largest is 0.055, compared with the uniform weight of 1/45 = 0.022.

The representations differ: unbounded weights can extrapolate in factor space, while bounded weights interpolate there. The intercept and covariate components remain outside this restriction.

#### Reading the comparison

`sim_gsynth` follows an IFE data generating process. In the unbounded fit, four of the five treated loadings lie inside the control hull and one lies outside.

The ATTs are 4.64 without the bound and 4.33 with it. The true ATT, the mean of `eff` over treated cells, is 5.46. The bounded estimate is 0.31 lower. That difference is 0.4 and 0.3 times the respective standard errors, 0.78 and 1.02 in this run.

Both estimates are below the truth, by 0.82 and 1.14, about 1.1 standard errors each. The bound does not bring the estimate closer to the truth in this simulation. The weights differ more than the ATTs: for four of the five treated units, bounded weights exceed 0.01 on 16 or fewer donors.

### Caveats

- The bound requires `time.component.from = "nevertreated"`, through `method = "gsynth"` or the equivalent IFE specification.
- Percentile-bootstrap intervals may under-cover when the true treated loading lies on the boundary of $\mathrm{conv}(\Lambda_{co})$. Inspect `loading.proj.resid` for poor constrained fit. It does not establish whether the true loading is on the boundary. Boundary-corrected inference is not implemented.
- The unit intercept $\alpha_i$ is not bounded. Since version 2.4.8, it is fitted jointly with the loadings when `force` is `"unit"` or `"two-way"`.
- Before version 2.4.7, the bound was dropped without a message in CV, fits without standard errors, parametric-bootstrap replicates, and `loo = TRUE` refits. Estimates, standard errors, and selected ranks can differ from earlier versions.
- Before version 2.4.8, the loadings were fitted without an intercept, which was then set to the residual mean. Under `"unit"` or `"two-way"`, the treated outcome level could change the loadings, ATT, and selected `gamma.loading`. On `sim_gsynth`, the bounded ATT above was 5.10 before version 2.4.8 and is 4.33 now. Fits with `"none"` or `"time"` are unchanged.

## CFE with never-treated controls

The complex fixed effects (CFE) estimator also supports `time.component.from = "nevertreated"`. It can add fixed effects, unit-specific trends through `Q.type`, or time-invariant covariates with time-varying coefficients through `Z` and `gamma`. See [Chapter @sec-cfe] for the CFE tutorial.

### Estimation

Set `method = "cfe"` and `time.component.from = "nevertreated"`. This example also includes unit-specific linear trends.

```{r cfe_nt_demo, eval=TRUE, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
out.cfe.nt <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id","time"),
                   method = "cfe", force = "two-way",
                   time.component.from = "nevertreated",
                   Q.type = "linear",
                   se = FALSE, CV = TRUE, r = c(0, 5),
                   parallel = TRUE, cores = 16)
```

```{r cfe-nt-summary}
cat("CFE + nevertreated: r.cv =", out.cfe.nt$r.cv,
    ", ATT =", round(out.cfe.nt$att.avg, 3), "\n")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
With `time.component.from = "nevertreated"`, CFE estimates factors from never-treated controls, as GSC does. It fits the additional CFE components on the control panel and projects them onto treated units. See [Chapter @sec-cfe].
:::

### Comparing GSC and CFE

The following comparison holds the estimation regime fixed and varies the model components. `fect_mspe()` reports prediction scores. It does not replace the treated-unit rank rule of Step 3.

```{r cfe_nt_vs_gsynth, eval=TRUE, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Model 1: gsynth (pure IFE, r = 2)
out.gsynth.comp <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id","time"),
                        method = "gsynth", force = "two-way",
                        r = 2, se = FALSE, CV = FALSE, max.iteration = 20000)

# Model 2: CFE + nevertreated with r = 2 only (equivalent to gsynth)
out.cfe.nt.comp <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id","time"),
                        method = "cfe", force = "two-way",
                        time.component.from = "nevertreated",
                        r = 2, se = FALSE, CV = FALSE, max.iteration = 20000)

# Model 3: CFE + nevertreated with r = 2 and linear trend (overspecified)
out.cfe.nt.lin <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id","time"),
                       method = "cfe", force = "two-way",
                       time.component.from = "nevertreated",
                       Q.type = "linear", r = 2, se = FALSE, CV = FALSE,
                       max.iteration = 20000)
```

```{r cfe_nt_mspe, eval=TRUE, cache=TRUE}
mspe.comp <- fect_mspe(list(gsynth_r2 = out.gsynth.comp,
                            CFE_r2 = out.cfe.nt.comp,
                            CFE_linear_r2 = out.cfe.nt.lin), seed = 1234)
print(mspe.comp$summary[, c("Model", "MSPE", "RMSE", "MAD")])
```

`sim_gsynth` follows an IFE data generating process with two factors. Models 1 and 2 fit that model using never-treated controls. Their MSPEs are 1.94 and 1.91, and their MADs are 0.538 and 0.541. Different iterative algorithms stop at slightly different solutions. On the full data, their ATTs agree to four decimals (5.5433).

Model 3 adds unit-specific linear trends absent from the data generating process. Its MSPE is 3.27, about 1.7 times that of Model 2. Rolling CV fits each held-out unit's trend using earlier periods and extrapolates it. Here the extra parameters increase prediction error.

`fect_mspe()` scores the full prediction: the intercept, unit and time effects, covariates, factors, and additional CFE terms. Before version 2.4.7, it scored these never-treated fits using only the factor component for GSC or 0 for CFE. Both CFE models then scored 110.33 regardless of specification.

## Inference

The default `vartype` is `"bootstrap"` for every method, including `method = "gsynth"`. Set `vartype = "parametric"` explicitly for GSC with few treated units. Its two-stage procedure targets the conditional prediction-error variance

$$
V_t = \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathrm{ATT}}_t - \mathrm{ATT}_t \mid \Lambda, F, X, D).
$$

It uses prediction errors from controls left out of the factor fit. Its limitations, including few controls and uncertainty from rank selection, are described in Step 4 of [Section @sec-gsynth-checks].

For the GSC parametric bootstrap, `para.error`, introduced in v2.4.2, selects the error resampling path. `"auto"` uses `"empirical"` on fully observed panels and `"ar"` when outcomes are missing. The other options are `"ar"`, the v2.4.1 behavior, `"empirical"`, and `"wild"`. See [Chapter @sec-inference] for the interaction of `vartype`, `ci.method`, and `para.error`, bootstrap mechanics, and the coverage study.

The jackknife is also available. Like the unit bootstrap, it relies on variation across units and does not solve the inference problem with few treated units.

```{r simJack, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE}
out2 <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth,  index = c("id","time"),
               method = "gsynth", force = "two-way",
               CV = TRUE, r = c(0, 5), se = TRUE,
               vartype = "jackknife",
               parallel = TRUE, cores = 16)

```

### Conformal intervals {#sec-gsynth-conformal}

Conformal intervals (`vartype = "conformal"`) are a second way to handle few treated units. The parametric bootstrap simulates each treated unit's prediction error from a model of the errors. Conformal inference instead treats each never-treated control in turn as if it had been treated at the same date, predicts it in the same way, and compares the treated units' prediction errors with the controls' (the Jackknife+ of @liuxu2026conformal). Under the conditions in [Section @sec-conformal-assumptions], each interval covers its effect with probability at least $1 -$ `alpha` in finite samples, with no model of the errors. [Chapter @sec-conformal] explains the method. This section shows how it fits the five checks.

The call below uses the rank the forward rule chose in Step 3, held fixed with `CV = FALSE`. With five treated units, `conformal.block = TRUE` gives the average effect an interval with a guarantee: it compares the five treated units, taken together, with nine blocks of five controls ([Section @sec-conformal-block]). The blocks are drawn at random, so set `seed`. The level is 90%: a 95% block interval needs at least 19 blocks, or 95 controls here, and with 45 controls it would be the whole real line.

```{r gsc-conformal, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE}
out.cf <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"),
               method = "gsynth", force = "two-way", r = 2, CV = FALSE,
               se = TRUE, vartype = "conformal", alpha = 0.1,
               conformal.block = TRUE, seed = 1234)
print(out.cf)
```

The block interval for the average effect runs from `r round(out.cf$est.avg[1, "CI.lower"], 2)` to `r round(out.cf$est.avg[1, "CI.upper"], 2)`. The 90% normal interval from the parametric bootstrap in Step 3 runs from `r round(out.fwd$est.avg[1, "ATT.avg"] - qnorm(0.95) * out.fwd$est.avg[1, "S.E."], 2)` to `r round(out.fwd$est.avg[1, "ATT.avg"] + qnorm(0.95) * out.fwd$est.avg[1, "S.E."], 2)`. The p-value, `r round(out.cf$est.avg[1, "p.value"], 2)`, is the smallest possible with nine blocks ($1/N$ with $N = 10$). There are no standard errors. When both intervals are reported and they disagree, the parametric one depends on the model of the errors, and the conformal one on the comparison with the controls.

The plot compares the two 90% intervals in each period after treatment.

```{r gsc-conformal-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2}
library(ggplot2)
post <- function(m) m[as.numeric(rownames(m)) >= 1, , drop = FALSE]
pb <- post(out.fwd$est.att)
cf <- post(out.cf$est.att)
z <- qnorm(0.95)
ci <- rbind(
  data.frame(t = as.numeric(rownames(pb)), att = pb[, "ATT"],
             lo = pb[, "ATT"] - z * pb[, "S.E."], hi = pb[, "ATT"] + z * pb[, "S.E."],
             type = "Parametric bootstrap"),
  data.frame(t = as.numeric(rownames(cf)), att = cf[, "ATT"],
             lo = cf[, "CI.lower"], hi = cf[, "CI.upper"],
             type = "Conformal (block Jackknife+)"))
ci$type <- factor(ci$type, levels = c("Parametric bootstrap", "Conformal (block Jackknife+)"))
ggplot(ci, aes(x = t, y = att, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, colour = type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), shape = 21,
                  fill = "white", size = 0.3, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey50", "#004a8c"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(x = "Periods since treatment", y = "Effect on Y (90% intervals)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

With nine blocks, each conformal interval is set by the most extreme of the nine blocks' errors at that date, so its width changes more from period to period than the parametric interval's. It is wider in `r with(ci, sum((hi - lo)[type != "Parametric bootstrap"] > (hi - lo)[type == "Parametric bootstrap"]))` of the 10 periods, most of all in periods 1, 5 and 8. In period 1 it includes zero, and the parametric interval, just above zero, does not.

Three of the five checks bear on the conformal guarantee.

- **Count the data (Step 1).** A finite interval at `alpha = 0.1` needs at least nine never-treated controls, and the block interval needs at least nine per treated unit.
- **Check overlap (Steps 2 and 3).** The guarantee needs the treated units to be no harder to predict than the controls. A treated unit that the donors cannot follow, or whose loadings lie far outside the controls', is the usual way this fails. The overlap checks give evidence on this condition, and `conformal.diag` adds pre-treatment intervals ([Section @sec-conformal-checks]).
- **Choose the rank (Step 3).** The guarantee assumes a rank fixed in advance. The forward rule chooses the rank from the treated units' pretreatment outcomes, and @liuxu2026conformal warn that tuning on the treated units' fit can break the guarantee. Passing the chosen rank with `CV = FALSE` does not change this. Report the intervals at nearby ranks as well:

```{r gsc-conformal-ranks, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE}
cf.near <- sapply(c(1, 3), function(r) {
  fit <- fect(Y ~ D + X1 + X2, data = sim_gsynth, index = c("id", "time"),
              method = "gsynth", force = "two-way", r = r, CV = FALSE,
              se = TRUE, vartype = "conformal", alpha = 0.1,
              conformal.block = TRUE, seed = 1234)
  fit$est.avg[1, c("ATT.avg", "CI.lower", "CI.upper")]
})
colnames(cf.near) <- c("r = 1", "r = 3")
round(cf.near, 2)
```

At one and three factors, the intervals are wider than at two, and all three exclude zero. Conformal intervals are also available for IFE-EM (`method = "ife"`) and matrix completion (`method = "mc"`), with the same conditions.

## Additional notes

Missing data, covariates, and the pretreatment window affect computation and the information available for estimation.

- **Unbalanced panels.** Missing control outcomes require iterative imputation and can increase computation time. Inspect the missing-data pattern before fitting. Removing units or periods changes the analysis sample and should be reported. GSC still estimates factors from never-treated controls and uses treated units' pretreatment outcomes to estimate their loadings.
- **Covariates.** Covariates add parameters and can increase the work needed for convergence. Choose them for the outcome model and inspect convergence.
- **`min.T0`.** This argument excludes treated units with too few pretreatment observations. For CV, it must be at least `r.max` + 2. A unit that meets it, for example with `min.T0 = 5`, can still have too few periods for the rank rule: Step 1 asks for about 15 when the candidate ranks go up to 5, and `fect_rank()` reports whether the window is long enough.

Cite @Xu2017 for GSC.

```bibtex
@article{Xu2017,
  title = {Generalized Synthetic Control Method: Causal Inference with Interactive Fixed Effects Models},
  author = {Xu, Yiqing},
  journal = {Political Analysis},
  volume = {25},
  number = {1},
  pages = {57--76},
  year = {2017}
}
```
